job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven and take the metro across Porto to an electricity grid operator. I'm a graduate engineer in the network planning team, so I check load forecasts, run simulations for new connections and draft reports for my team lead, Dona Teresa. I studied electrical engineering at the university here, and my final project was about solar panels and the local grid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the work matters, because when it goes wrong whole neighbourhoods lose power. What tires me is the long reports and the long meetings. I share a flat with a friend, Marta, who works in marketing, and I have lunch at my grandmother's every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not magic. At work I'd keep using it for small things and not trust it with anything that touches the grid. A bad forecast doesn't give you a typo, it gives you a blackout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. Power grids are slow, regulated and full of safety rules, so change comes carefully. I have no debt, about eight months of savings and a decent salary, and my parents would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: learn the planning software, take the grid-code training and keep doing site visits to substations. I'd save 350 euros a month and maybe buy a small flat in four or five years. I'd also keep using the AI tool for first drafts of reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a steady, well-lit road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What do you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to tidy my report drafts and to explain a technical standard in simpler words. I check everything against the original. Once it gave me a wrong voltage limit, and I'm glad I checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marta, your flatmate, about the hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta it's a handy tool, like a good spreadsheet, and she'd say her marketing team already uses it daily. Her job is more exposed than mine. I'd say that gently, because she's worried.

Save **350 euros** a month toward a small flat.
Keep using the AI tool for first **drafts** of reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change a lot of the desk work, and I'd say that calmly to colleagues. At work I'd propose a short training for the whole team, so nobody is left behind. Forecasting and report writing are the first jobs a machine will do well, and we should decide who checks them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a bit uneasy. Load forecasts and simulations are exactly what these tools do well, and a team of six could become a team of four. The grid itself will still need engineers who understand the physics, and that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in power systems and data tools so I can check the machines rather than compete with them. I'd also ask Dona Teresa for field work and design reviews, which need a person. I'd save 450 euros a month and keep my flat share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. I'm not shaken, I just keep it in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks would software take first in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-pass forecasts and the standard reports. They take me hours and a tool can do them in minutes. What I can't hand over is deciding what's safe to connect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior colleagues who joined with me, and an older planner, Senhor Alberto, who struggles with new software. I'd try to help him, but I can't stop a restructure.

steps.text: Use the forecasting tool daily and check its results by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules for the energy sector in particular. At work I'd back a plan that keeps humans in charge of grid decisions. Whoever runs the grid has to be someone we can ask questions and hold to account, not a black box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious. If thinking work goes in two years, then planning, forecasting and reporting go with it, and a grid operator with fewer engineers might not need new graduates. The hands-on side of the grid, like substations and cables, would take about three years longer, so I'd lean there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as much as I can, maybe 800 euros a month, and ask to move to the field team, which maintains substations. I'd get my safety certificates and take a technician's course in high-voltage work. I'd also cut my spending on eating out and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I have some control. It's a tight feeling in my chest rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dona Teresa straight away and ask where the team will be in two years. I'd get my high-voltage certificate within the first six months. I'd also tell my parents my plan so they don't hear it from someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandmother over Sunday lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'm learning to climb poles, in a way. She'd laugh and say I was always stubborn. She grew up in a village where the electricity came late, so she'd see the grid as precious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people start now. At work I'd suggest a long-term plan for staff, covering retraining and what roles we keep. Five years is a window, and I'd rather walk through it than watch it close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy rather than scared. By 2031 a lot of planning will be automated, but regulation will still ask for a named engineer to sign off. I could be the one who signs, and that gives me a bit of calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to become good at both the physics and the tools. I'd do a part-time master's in power systems with machine learning, save 500 euros a month and keep going to site visits. In year three I'd decide whether to move up into management or deeper into the technical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit nervous, a bit curious, mostly steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on years give me time to build a field profile, so I'm not only a desk person. I'd learn how substations are built and maintained. That makes me more useful and harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at the grid operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they let me. Energy will need people, even if the work changes. If they cut graduates, I'd look at renewable developers or the regulator, who need people who understand the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and the energy sector will need people who understand both grids and software. At work I'd argue for regular retraining days. Ten years is enough time to build a good career twice, if employers and governments don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pretty calm. At 32 I could be leading a team that manages automated grids, and energy has a long, steady demand. I'd worry more about the cost of living and housing in Porto than about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, build my skills, and buy a small flat. I'd finish a master's part-time, move into a role that mixes engineering and data, and keep using AI tools more as they improve. I'd also volunteer for a project teaching solar basics at a local school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal career with a few big changes in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you knew it was ten years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same plans, but slower. I'd still save, I'd still study, and I'd use the tools more each year. The difference is I wouldn't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children and a house in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I'd want a flat and maybe a child around 30, and a partner who works too. The date doesn't change that, but it makes me want a job that can survive it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm the kind of person who plans, and two years leaves very little room to plan anything. What would help is staff plans from employers, paid retraining time and rules that keep a named human responsible for the grid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that grids touch everyone, so people in my field feel a duty. If the lights go out because someone trusted a program too fast, nobody will remember it was a clever program. They'll remember who signed.

headlineQuote: I'm the kind of person who plans, and two years leaves very little room to plan anything.
portrait: Aisha is **22**, an electrical engineering graduate working in network planning at a grid operator in Porto.
She has no debt, about eight months saved and parents who would help, and she shares a flat with a friend.
She is centre and pragmatic, **blames** nobody, and wants rules that keep a named human responsible.
She is steady: she moves once change is proven, and plans to shift toward **field work** and a master's.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because two years leaves very little room to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Employer **staff plans**, paid retraining time and rules that keep a named engineer responsible for the grid.
